overview: My research concerns the planning of operations and service systems. I study scheduling, capacity and resource allocation, including decisions made across facilities, organizations and time periods. Applications include industrial operations, supply chains, healthcare, humanitarian logistics and public infrastructure.

I develop mathematical models and algorithms to understand these decisions and compare alternatives. I am particularly interested in combining optimization with learning, coordinating investments with operating plans, and preparing systems for uncertain demand and disruption.

algorithms.question: How can models, computation and learning work together to improve complex decisions?
paragraphs: I develop mathematical programming models, decomposition methods and hybrid algorithms. Many of the problems I study involve assignments and schedules that depend on one another. I look for formulations that retain these dependencies and can still be solved within the time available for planning.

My interests in learning include adaptive operator selection, the allocation of computational effort and methods that transfer between problem settings. I want to understand when a learned strategy remains useful as demand, capacity or other conditions change.

I am also interested in language models that help translate operational requirements into mathematical formulations, propose solution methods or explain solver output. This work raises questions about checking model validity, using solver feedback and deciding where human judgment is needed. Quantum–classical hybrid optimization is a further exploratory interest; comparisons with established classical methods are essential.
questions: Which mathematical structures enable useful decomposition or learning across decision problems?
How should a planning system allocate computation when time and data are limited?
How can AI proposals be checked, corrected and compared with reliable optimization baselines?

maritime.question: How should connected operations and technology investments be coordinated across a system?
paragraphs: Production, inventories, transport and service decisions often compete for the same resources. A schedule that works for one facility may cause delays elsewhere. I am interested in planning these activities jointly and in decomposition methods that preserve their timing and capacity constraints.

Coordination also depends on who makes decisions and what information they share. My interests include cooperation between organizations, purchasing and service commitments, and the distribution of costs and benefits. One question is when additional capacity is more useful than better coordination.

Automation and electrification add investment decisions to these operating problems. Equipment, charging capacity, energy supply, maintenance and workforce requirements affect how a system can be run. I am interested in phased adoption and shared infrastructure, and in how their value changes under different operating policies.
questions: When should sourcing, processing, storage, transport and service be planned jointly?
How do information and incentives affect coordination across organizations?
How should equipment adoption and supporting infrastructure be evaluated together with operating policies?

resilience.question: How can systems prepare for change while balancing service, resources and environmental goals?
paragraphs: I study how operations can prepare for disruption and recover as new information becomes available. This includes deciding where to hold inventory or reserve capacity, which alternatives to keep available and when to revise an existing plan.

Flexibility has a cost. Alternative suppliers, backup resources and revised service commitments may reduce disruption losses but require investment or impose costs on other organizations. I am interested in how these trade-offs change with uncertainty and how disruptions spread through a supply chain.

These questions also arise in healthcare, humanitarian response and public services, where delays and resource shortages affect access to care or assistance. My interests include models that account for service reliability and fairness alongside cost, energy use, emissions and material recovery.
questions: Where does flexibility create the greatest value before a disruption?
Which commitments should change as information evolves, and which should remain stable?
How can operating decisions account for service, equity, energy and environmental consequences together?

cases.title: A smaller model for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A compact berth-scheduling formulation supports Benders decomposition and column generation for larger planning problems.
cases.question: Can a smaller formulation solve larger berth-scheduling problems?
cases.approach: This study develops a mixed-integer formulation for dynamic, discrete berth scheduling. Two-dimensional decision variables and a simplified vessel-sequencing structure reduce model complexity. Benders decomposition and column generation build on the formulation to address larger instances.
cases.evidence: The computational study compares the formulation with five mathematical models and three metaheuristics. It reports solutions for instances with more than 260 vessels within two hours under the tested settings, alongside sensitivity analysis of operational parameters.
cases.meaning: A compact formulation reduces the computation needed to represent vessel assignments and service order. In this study, that reduction makes larger instances accessible to exact optimization and decomposition methods.
cases.connection: The formulation and decomposition ideas may also apply to problems that combine resource assignments with sequencing.
cases.futureQuestion: How can compact formulations be extended to coordinated resource decisions when berthing, handling and downstream service interact?

cases.title: Coordinating inbound and outbound trucks
cases.summary: Sequential optimization and pricing-guided search address coupled truck services, freight transfers and departure timing.
cases.question: How can inbound unloading, internal freight transfer and outbound loading be scheduled together?
cases.approach: The study formulates coordinated truck service as a mixed-integer linear program. Its objective accounts for waiting, handling, temporary storage and delay costs. A sequential fix-and-optimize framework constructs service plans in batches that respect precedence relationships; a second framework uses pricing-guided search.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments compare the model and both solution frameworks. Sensitivity analyses examine how scheduling parameters affect costs and operations.
cases.meaning: The results show why truck schedules need to account for unloading, freight transfer and outbound loading together: changing one service can alter whether the rest of the plan is feasible.
cases.connection: This work motivates my interest in coordinating schedules across processing, transfer and service stages.
cases.futureQuestion: When should additional processing or storage capacity be preferred to improved coordination of inbound and outbound operations?

cases.title: Learning which scheduling operators to use
cases.summary: Thompson Sampling adapts operator selection while repair and exact evaluation address schedule feasibility and accuracy.
cases.question: Can a truck-scheduling search procedure learn which operators are useful as the search progresses?
cases.approach: The Hybridized Thompson Sampling Hyperheuristic combines evolutionary search with an adaptive operator-selection controller. A repair-and-penalty mechanism handles inbound–outbound precedence constraints. Fast approximate fitness evaluation supports exploration, while exact optimization refines schedule evaluation.
cases.evidence: On the reported benchmark instances, the algorithm produces solutions comparable with exact optimization for small problems and improves on the comparison metaheuristics. The paper reports improvements of up to approximately 24% and an average runtime of 186.71 seconds across its experimental setting.
cases.meaning: The algorithm learns which search operators to use while retaining checks on schedule feasibility. Approximate evaluation reduces search time, and exact optimization improves the accuracy of the final evaluation.
cases.connection: A next question is whether the learned search strategies remain useful under different demand patterns and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: Can adaptive search strategies transfer between demand patterns and facilities while preserving feasible schedules?

cases.title: Combining adaptive search with exact optimization
cases.summary: A berth-scheduling hyperheuristic adapts genetic operators and periodically applies problem-specific exact improvement.
cases.question: How can a search algorithm adapt to the berth-scheduling problem while retaining the benefits of exact optimization?
cases.approach: The Hyperheuristic Hybridized with Exact Optimization addresses dynamic, discrete berth allocation and scheduling. It chooses genetic operators according to their observed performance and periodically applies berth-specific exact optimization procedures to improve candidate schedules.
cases.evidence: Computational comparisons examine the algorithm against exact-optimization-inspired methods and established metaheuristics. Component experiments investigate the contribution of hyperheuristic control and hybridization. Scenario analysis considers berth availability, vessel arrival intensity and departure-delay penalties.
cases.meaning: The algorithm adapts its search operators and uses exact optimization to improve individual berth schedules. The experiments test the contributions of both components.
cases.connection: I am interested in how to divide computation between broad search and exact improvement in other scheduling problems.
cases.futureQuestion: How should limited computation be divided between broad search and structured exact improvement as a planning problem changes?

cases.title: Evaluating rail-crossing closure decisions
cases.summary: An optimization framework considers safety, economic and environmental effects alongside delay and maintenance costs.
cases.question: Which rail crossings should close when safety, delay, cost and environmental effects are considered together?
cases.approach: The study develops an optimization model that includes safety, economic and environmental benefits as well as traffic-delay and maintenance implications. A sorting-inspired heuristic addresses the resulting decision problem. Computational experiments use crossings in Florida.
cases.evidence: The paper compares the heuristic with an exact method and tests how model inputs affect closure decisions. An associated FDOT technical report describes the project and its analyses.
cases.meaning: The model compares closure choices using the same set of safety, economic, environmental and delay measures. This makes the trade-offs between candidate crossings explicit.
cases.connection: Related questions arise when public agencies prioritize infrastructure under uncertain safety, access and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: How can infrastructure prioritization represent uncertainty and changes in access, exposure and operating conditions?

cases.title: Recovering ship schedules under environmental constraints
cases.summary: Multi-objective optimization examines the tension between schedule recovery, monetary losses and speed-reduction incentives.
cases.question: How should a shipping line recover from disruption when sailing faster conflicts with environmental rules or incentives?
cases.approach: This collaborative study models monetary losses and port-arrival delays as competing objectives. It incorporates voluntary speed-reduction incentive programs, emission-control requirements and multiple recovery options. The solution method combines dynamic secant approximation with an epsilon-constraint approach.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use the South East Asia Pendulum shipping route, with sensitivity analysis exploring how different settings affect recovery choices.
cases.meaning: Reducing arrival delay can increase costs or forfeit a speed-reduction incentive. Comparing alternative recovery plans shows these trade-offs before a shipping line chooses a response.
cases.connection: This work motivates questions about which service commitments to preserve during recovery and how much flexibility to prepare beforehand.
cases.futureQuestion: Which commitments should be preserved during recovery, and where does flexibility provide the greatest value before a disruption?

approach: I want students to understand what a method assumes, why they would use it and how to interpret its results. In optimization courses, writing a model and explaining its limitations are as important as obtaining a solution.

I begin with small examples that students can work through by hand, then move to implementation and comparison. Projects ask students to choose a method, test their code and explain what they learn from the results.

Students arrive with different mathematical and programming backgrounds. Guided examples, targeted review and intermediate project submissions help them work toward the same course expectations with increasing independence.
teaching.mentoring: I have mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers and served as an external master’s thesis committee member. I help students define a manageable question, check their computational work and explain their findings and limitations.

agenda.title: Integrated operations and supply chains
agenda.text: How should sourcing, production, storage, distribution and service be planned across facilities? I am interested in shared capacity, shifting bottlenecks and the information and incentives needed for coordination. A related question is how investment choices change the operating policies available later.

agenda.title: Resilience and decisions under uncertainty
agenda.text: I am interested in the value of reserve capacity, alternative suppliers and flexible service arrangements. The aim is to compare what should be prepared in advance with what can be changed during a disruption, including the costs of revising commitments and the effects on service.

agenda.title: Learning, language models and optimization
agenda.text: My interests include AI-assisted model formulation, learning-guided search and algorithms that use solver feedback. Questions include whether methods transfer across applications, how to allocate computation and how people should work with analytical agents. Proposed methods need checks of feasibility, solution quality and runtime.

agenda.title: Electrification, automation and energy-aware operations
agenda.text: I am interested in planning equipment and charging investments together with scheduling, maintenance and energy use. This includes phased adoption, shared infrastructure and workforce requirements. The question is how these choices affect cost, service and environmental performance over time.

agenda.title: Healthcare, humanitarian and public-service systems
agenda.text: Healthcare and emergency services must allocate limited resources to needs that vary over time. I am interested in scheduling and allocation methods that account for timeliness, reliability and access, including how services should respond to disruption and how different groups are affected.

currentWork.title: Integrated scheduling and shared-resource allocation
currentWork.text: I am studying scheduling problems in which processing tasks, vehicle movements and shared resources must be coordinated. The models examine completion time, resource requirements and energy use. I am also investigating how to decompose these problems without losing the timing constraints between activities.

currentWork.title: Emergency response and healthcare scheduling
currentWork.text: My current work includes resource-constrained planning for flood response and healthcare services. I am investigating compact models, rolling planning and the selective revision of schedules when conditions change or computation time is limited.

currentWork.title: Infrastructure electrification and implementation
currentWork.text: My shore-power work examines whether infrastructure commitments lead to equipment readiness and use. It considers the records needed to assess implementation and how operating activity should inform investment decisions and environmental reporting.

currentWork.title: AI tools for searching technical guidance
currentWork.text: I have built a local research prototype that retrieves information from public transportation-agency manuals and returns summaries with source references. I am using it to study how technical guidance can be searched and interpreted. It has not been deployed as an agency decision system.

evaluation.title: Mathematical structure and feasibility
evaluation.text: A model must represent the resource, timing and precedence relationships that determine whether a plan can be carried out. I am interested in compact formulations and decompositions that reduce computational effort while retaining these relationships.

evaluation.title: Computational comparisons
evaluation.text: Algorithms need to be compared under stated computational budgets and operating conditions. Solution quality, feasibility, time to a usable plan and sensitivity to problem size provide complementary evidence; a single best objective does not describe every planning requirement.

evaluation.title: Operating consequences
evaluation.text: The purpose of a computational result is to clarify a decision. Relevant questions include how a plan changes service, resource utilization, energy use or exposure to disruption, and which assumptions determine those effects.
